newsitem.title: USA: As tax filing deadline nears, U.S. IRS under fire.
newsitem.headline: As tax filing deadline nears, U.S. IRS under fire.

text.p: At least since the biblical St. Matthew -- a tax collector before he was a saint -- the tax man has been unpopular.

Internal Revenue Service Commissioner Margaret Milner Richardson knows how St. Matthew felt. As the U.S. April 15 tax filing deadline looms, Richardson is frustrated at an avalanche of cricism of the agency Americans love to hate.
Among the IRS-bashing headlines of recent months:
-- A $4 billion IRS computer modernisation programme was a flop.
-- The IRS has "browsers" who rifle tax returns without authorisation.

The income tax collection agency stands accused of auditing people for political reasons, not balancing its own books, and -- while insisting that taxpayers being audited produce every little receipt -- stashing some of its own files where no one can find them.
The IRS "flunked its own audit," Sen. John Glenn, an Ohio Democrat, said last week.

A bipartisan commission headed by Sen. Bob Kerry, Democrat of Nebraska and Representative Rob Portman, an Ohio Republican, has been holding hearings on the IRS and plans to recommend revamping the agency later this year.

There is even a movement to abolish the IRS. One of Republican Bob Dole's sure-fire applause lines during his failed 1996 campaign for the presidency was "end the IRS as we know it." But only about a fifth of Americans in a recent survey said they thought the IRS should be abolished.

Richardson, who was named commissioner by President (Bill) Clinton in 1993 and is leaving at the end of the current tax filing season, concedes many problems exist but thinks a lot of the criticism is unconstructive IRS-bashing.
"I think a number of gratuitous comments have been made merely to get a headline or get attention," she told Reuters.
"We are an agency that touches the lives of almost everyone, which gives us a special responsibility," she said. "But it also makes us a surrogate for people's frustrations."

Richardson also thinks some of the oversight is overdone. She says the IRS has been the subject of 140 evaluations by the General Accounting Office in the last four years, and more than 275 IRS employees are working full-time just to help the GAO conduct the oversight.
In its most recent report, the GAO said it checked five IRS facilities and found it could not locate about 6,400 tapes that could contain taxpayer data.

David Keating, executive vice president of the National Taxpayers' Union -- a citizen's watchdog organisation -- said no one need pity the IRS. "I wouldn't," he said. "I think the scrutiny is good, and probably long overdue."

But in defence of the beleaguered agency, Keating added: "I think it is fair to say the agency is blamed for things that are not its fault, like the insanely complicated tax law. I don't care how good an agency is, how can you enforce a law fairly when no one knows what it means?"
Congress writes the U.S. income tax law, which has developed a byzantine complexity over the years, in part due to amendments intended to make it more fair.

"If you go back in history, tax collectors were not that popular," Richardson said, alluding to some contemporaries of St. Matthew who, according to biblical accounts, scrupulously avoided "tax collectors and other sinners."
"I think most people understand what we do, and understand that we don't write the laws, we just enforce them," Richardson said.

And while there are proposals to "simplify" the tax code by replacing the income tax with a "flat" tax rate or a national sales tax, such changes are considered unlikely. Overhauling the IRS has been getting more attention than overhauling the tax law.

A 17-member, bipartisan National Commission on Restructuring the Internal Revenue Service has been holding hearings for months and will present its report this summer. It is expected to recommend a new IRS management structure, perhaps such as a corporate-style board of directors.

The commission could also propose a plan to reach 100 percent electronic filing of tax returns, which would reduce filing errors and unwarranted audits. And, the commission may "take a shot at a chunk of tax simplification" for working-class Americans, chief of staff Jeff Trinka said.

In a potentially more explosive investigation, Congress' Joint Committee on Taxation is examining reports that the IRS is targeting conservative critics of Clinton for audits. Richardson fiercely denies this.
"I personally do not believe that any organisation has any reason to question the propriety of why we are doing an audit," Richardson said.

But some organisations that are being audited, such as the conservative Heritage Foundation and the National Rifle Association, do have questions. The NRA and the Heritage Foundation enjoy tax-exempt status, which means supporters can deduct donations.

"Do I think it's political? Well, do you believe it's a coincidence that less than two weeks after Clinton blamed us publicly for being instrumental in changing the majority (from Democrat to Republican) in Congress, we heard we were being audited?" said Bill Powers, an NRA spokesman.
